text: You've already run az login and az account show. Here's the gap most beginners hit immediately: a real administrator's account almost always touches more than one subscription, and the CLI defaults to whichever one it thinks is current — which is not always the one you actually want.

az account list shows every subscription your account can reach, in a readable table. az account set, with --subscription and either a name or an ID, switches the active one. Everything you run after that targets that subscription until you switch again. Running a command against the wrong subscription because nobody checked first is one of the most common real mistakes administrators make.

Zoom out, and the commands you've already typed share one shape: az, then a command group like vm, group, storage, or network, then an action, then parameters. Once a handful of groups click, you can often guess the command you need for a new service before ever looking it up — the same discoverability idea behind PowerShell's Verb-Noun pattern, coming up in Lesson 23.

Every az command returns JSON by default. --output table is what you reach for while working interactively, because it's readable. --output tsv strips that down to plain tab-separated rows with no headers, which is exactly what a script loops over cleanly. --query is a different tool entirely: it applies a JMESPath expression to the raw JSON first, picking out just the fields you want, like name and VM size, before --output ever decides how to display them.

Put them together and az vm list with a --query building a small Name-and-Size object, piped through --output table, turns forty rows of dense JSON into exactly the three columns you asked for. Query picks what comes back. Output decides how it looks. Next: using that same pattern to run a full resource lifecycle from the command line, start to finish.
